senses: A children's ball game played in the street, the aim being to throw the ball against the opposite kerb and catch it on the rebound.
ety: From kerb + -y.
examples: It's dusk and there are a lot of kids out playing kerby and tag and football. For a December night, the weather isn't bad.
I'd play kerby in the street for hours looking up at contrails stretching across grey slate skies, wishing I was on a plane too, jetting away to somewhere else.
The heat from the tarmac refracted the light and disturbed the vision of the children as they persisted in their game of kerby.

senses: Food products made from leavened grain flour, which may not be consumed on Passover.
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew חָמֵץ (khaméts).
examples: The eating of chametz (leavened products) is explicitly prohibited on Passover (Exod. 12:19–20; 13:3), for the Israelites “took their dough before it was leavened” (Exod. 12:34) and left Egypt in great haste.
A chametz-free total environment is the Passover goal, so any place where chametz was or might have been used during the year is thoroughly checked and cleaned lest any chametz has been left behind.

senses: In the psychoanalytic theory of Wilhelm Reich, a form of sexual energy or life force distributed throughout the universe and available for collection, storage, and further use.
ety: Blend of organism + hormone, after German Orgon.
examples: In the present report I shall describe the methods of quantitative measurement of the orgone by means of the electroscope and the thermometer.
So, boys, when those hot licks play over your balls and prick and dart up your ass like an invisible blue blow torch of orgones, in the words of T. J. Watson, Think.

senses: A hot, wet medicated cloth or sponge applied externally.
ety: From Middle English, from Latin stūpa, variant of stuppa.
examples: And get your plasters, and your warm stupes ready.

senses: Made of, pertaining to, or resembling chitin.
ety: From chitin + -ous.
examples: The Ra'zac landed in front of him and jutted out its neck. Eragon recoiled as a short, thick beak appeared from within the depths of its hood. The chitinous appendage snapped shut just short of his right eye.
Not to mention you were too much of a scaredy cat to kill one of those chitinous shit-heads with your axe, my grandmother is less of a pussy than you and she’s gotten several painful diseases!

senses: A windstorm characterized by strong, straight-line winds.
ety: Learned borrowing from Spanish derecho (“straight”). First used by Gustavus Detlef Hinrichs in 1888, apparently coined to distinguish the winds from tornadoes, which rotate; compare tornado. Doublet of direct.
examples: Derechos have winds as powerful as those of some hurricanes and tornadoes. "Derecho" comes from the Spanish word meaning "straight."

senses: Having or showing confidence or trust in another person.
In confidence; as if with trust.
ety: By surface analysis, confide + -ing.
examples: Effingham was by nature indolent, confiding, and, at times, impetuous and indiscreet; but Marmaduke was uniformly equable, penetrating, and full of activity and enterprise.
Those eyes especially struck Eugene, and when he thought of Liza he always saw those clear, mild, confiding eyes.
Not having a confiding relationship with one's husband was, however, associated with elevated risk for symptoms of anxiety.

senses: A perennial European herb, Nasturtium officinale, that grows in freshwater streams; used in salads and as a garnish.
A similar plant, Nasturtium microphyllum.
ety: From Middle English water cresse, water-kresse, watercrasse, water cars, equivalent to water + cress. Cognate with West Frisian wetterkers (“watercress”), Dutch waterkers (“watercress”), German Wasserkresse (“waterkress”), Swedish vattenkrasse (“watercress”).
examples: A spring wells up in the centre of the village, and watercress beds lie beside the stream running alongside the main street.

senses: Incontrovertible; demonstrably true or certain.
Being a style of argument in which a person presents their reasoning as categorically true, even if it is not necessarily so.
ety: From the Latin apodīcticus (“proving clearly”, “demonstrative”), from the Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτικός (apodeiktikós, “affording proof”, “demonstrative”), from ἀποδείκνυμι (apodeíknumi, “to demonstrate”). In turn, from ἀπο- (apo-, “separate, without”), and δεικτικός (deiktikós, “capable of proof”).
examples: No religion has ever yet owed its prevalence to ‘apodictic certainty’.
The orca spoke in the odd grammatical tense used either to describe dreams, or to make statements so true they were apodictic, such as "All things die" or "Before my conception I did not exist."
Don’t be so apodictic! You haven’t considered several facets of the question.

senses: To assemble from thin sheets glued together to make a thicker sheet.
To cover (something flat, usually paper) in adhesive protective plastic.
To form (metal etc.) into a thin plate, as by rolling.
To cause to separate into thin plates or layers; to divide into thin plates.
ety: First attested in 1666; borrowed from New Latin laminātus, perfect passive participle of laminō (attested since the first quarter of the 16th century), from Latin lāmina (“thin sheet of metal/other material”), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3).
examples: We'll laminate the piece of wood with grain going in different directions to make a really strong hull for the boat.
We laminated the printouts so we could use them as signage.

senses: The study of the fate of the remains of organisms after they die, especially the study of fossilization.
ety: From tapho- (from Ancient Greek τάφος (táphos, “grave”)) + -nomy.
examples: Whilst there is some credit in distinguishing between taphonomies for thick-shelled forms and thin-shelled forms in shallower facies, these forms occur in both phacopids and homalonotids.
Some cases may have an innocent explanation based in taphonomy, the processes by which bodies are preserved over long spans of time.

senses: Coarse, dry breadcrumbs used in Japanese cuisine.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese パン粉 (panko).
examples: Japanese "Panko" bread crumbs upgrade the quality of shrimp and other frozen prepared foods with their exceptionally crisp, yet tender, bite. (Photo courtesy of National Sea Products.)
Sprinkle stuffed side evenly with panko.
But, she added, more modern interpretations could include anything from rhubarb and blueberries to panko, goat cheese and broccoli.

senses: The ability to do things without occupying the mind with the low level details required.
The process of one thing automatically following another.
ety: From automatic + -ity.
examples: No, donations and loans absolutely are not a means, with any automaticity, of getting a peerage, but they are not a bar to getting a peerage, and to some extent that is what we exist for.

The Committee's proposal for automatic registration would represent a significant shift away from the present system of elector-led application and voluntary registration, to a system of automaticity with an opt out.

senses: Especially, such objects that are collectibles, such as (originally) cheap publications (e.g., pamphlets, brochures), single-use packaging from packaged goods, and giveaway or throwaway trinkets.
Published single-sheet or single-page documents which are meant to be thrown away after one use.
Transitory audiovisual matter not intended to be retained or preserved.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερᾰ (ephḗmeră), neuter plural form of ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros).
examples: Now the model sits on a shelf in York's 'Warehouse' (known these days as the 'North Shed'), together with racks full of lamps, cutlery, and other ephemera from half-forgotten railway companies of long ago.
I have no interest in the sensational ephemera of the Press.

senses: Emmer wheat (Triticum turgidum).
ety: Borrowed from Italian farro. Doublet of far.
examples: All three farros are sold as a whole grain.

senses: The scrotum.
ety: Clipping of scrotum. The term may be related in some ways to North Germanic, as the senses are semantically identical to the similarly sounding Swedish skrutt and Icelandic skrjóður (“scrotum, scrap, old useless person”),
examples: Bring out your broadsword. / There's the hydra. / Slice his throat! / And grab his scrote.
If you just followed this show on the blogs, you would think I was just running around town, cutting people open from scrote to sternum, wearing their skin as a trophy.

senses: A soldier equipped for rapid movement; also, any of several light infantry regiments, especially in France.
A servant or attendant.
A hotel messenger, especially in France.
A hunter or huntsman.
A dish of meat cooked in a sauce containing mushrooms, shallots and white wine.
ety: Borrowed from French chasseur. Doublet of chaser.
examples: The chasseur of the Hôtel Récamier (whom he knew far too well) was approaching them at a run.

senses: A stub, especially a stub of undeveloped corn or fruit or nipple.
A small protuberance, bud, bump, or knob.
ety: Perhaps nub + -in.
examples: As an avid button collector, I have had to develop an efficient way of removing the nubbin of thread from the buttonhole.
She walks to the next room, a little larger, holding a double bed. The shade is half drawn, and low light gives each nubbin of the bedspread a shadow.

senses: The process of having something fitted again, repaired or restored.
ety: From re- + fit.
examples: The ship required a refit before setting out again.

At the start, the team removed the sides and the ceiling panels, alongside the seats. They then stripped out the cabling that runs through the carriage. Once that was done, the carriage would be ready for the refit.

senses: To make (someone or something) neat; to arrange (people or things) in an orderly, tidy way; to tidy.
To engage in activity that arranges someone or something in an orderly, tidy way.
ety: From neat + -en.
examples: She made a frantic attempt to neaten her hair.
Don't mind me if I neaten while you talk.

senses: A young salmon after its first return from the sea.
ety: From Middle English grills, grilles, of unknown origin. Cognate with Scots grils, grissill, girls (“young salmon”). Compare English grawl, Scots grawl, graulse (“young salmon, grilse”).
examples: In our own tongue salmon are fry as babies, parr as children, smolt as adolescents, and grilse as adults.

senses: More fully neroli oil or oil of neroli: an essential oil distilled from the blossoms of the bitter orange or Seville orange (Citrus × aurantium subsp. amara) used to make perfumes.
ety: Borrowed from French néroli (“neroli”), from Nerola, a town and comune in the Metropolitan City of Rome, Lazio, Italy. Marie Anne de La Trémoille, princesse des Ursins (1642–1722), Princess of Nerola but originally from France, is thought to have made neroli popular as a fragrance in her country of birth around 1670. The word is cognate with Italian (obsolete) nerola, neroli.
examples: Bouquet is the white curd soap perfumed with bergamot, oils of cloves, sassafras, thyme, and neroli, and coloured with brown ochre.

senses: A puzzle box solved with a passcode.
ety: Blend of cryptology + codex, coined in The Da Vinci Code (2003); see quotations.
examples: With an embossed cover, vellum pages and brooding, mysterious artwork, this tome has a rich, premium feel. Careful readers can use the enclosed UV light and cryptex to reveal secrets that remain hidden from view.

For immediate gratification, you can also hit up his Etsy Store; the Cryptex box (Note that it's for PLANS only, you'll need to cut and make it yourself) looks like a great gift for the smartest egg in your family.
Morphing Morphology: This cryptex (a vault used to hide secret messages) allows visitors to turn five wheels to line up the various parts of eight different trees found in North America.

senses: A national (or group) policy of non-interaction with other nations (or groups).
ety: From isolation + -ism.
examples: Many hope the period of American isolationism and country-first populism under President Trump will give way to an era of renewed U.S. global leadership and embrace of multilateralism to tackle common challenges.

senses: The behavior of a buffoon; foolishness, silliness.
ety: From buffoon + -ery.
examples: The Temperance Reform was too serious a matter for trifling jokes and buffooneries.
Preamble is a hard-boiled steel commuter built for comfort, durability, and buffoonery on pavement and gravel.

senses: The driver of a packhorse.
A packhorse; a beast of burden.
ety: From Middle English, from Old French sommetier (“pack-horse driver”), from Late Latin *sagmatarius, from Latin sagma, from Ancient Greek σάγμα (ságma, “pack-saddle”).
examples: Persuade me rather to be slave and sumpter / To this detested groom.

senses: Resembling bile, especially in color.
Peevishly ill-humored, irritable or bad tempered; irascible.
ety: From French bilieux, from Latin bīliōsus (“full of bile”), from bīlis (“bile”) + -ōsus (“full of”).
examples: Does money fail?—come to my mint—coin paper, Till gold be at a discount, and ashamed To show his bilious face, go purge himself, In emulation of her vestal whiteness.
The business-center of Schoenstrom took up one side of one block, facing the railroad. It was a row of one-story shops covered with galvanized iron, or with clapboards painted red and bilious yellow.

senses: Of a book or other work: the end.
ety: From Middle English finis, from Latin fīnis (“end; limit”). Doublet of fin, fine, and finish.
examples: He had gone through the work from the title-page to the finis at least forty times, and had just commenced it over again.

senses: Afflicted, or looking as if afflicted, with mange.
Worn and squalid-looking; bedraggled or decrepit.
Contemptible, despicable, low.
ety: From mange + -y.
examples: We stayed in a really mangy hotel in New York.
Specter Knight: 'YOUR QUEST TO BECOME KING OF CARDS HAS NOT... GONE UNNOTICED.' / King Knight: 'AH, WORD HAS REACHED THE SLUMS, HAS IT? AM I TO TRAVEL WITH AN ENTOURAGE OF MANGY BEGGARS, NOW?'

senses: The state of being degenerate (in all senses).
ety: From degener(ate) + -acy.
examples: Inveterate abuse of drinking in nonhereditarily disposed persons creates a degeneracy like the hereditary.

senses: The record of a single event or item.
ety: Back formation from annals, borrowed from Middle French, from Latin annales (“annals”), from annus (“year”).
examples: In deathless annal! deathless deeds inspire:

senses: A kind of hat with a high conical or cylindrical crown and a saucer-shaped brim, highly embroidered, made of plush felt.
A mixed drink with coffee liqueur and cream.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish sombrero (“hat”), from sombra (“shadow, shade”) + -ero, literally, "shade-maker". The drink was named after the hat.
examples: Beatrice looked up and saw a man standing before her; the huge sombrero overshadowed his face, but the light of the lamp shone on a large and glittering knife in his girdle.

senses: To reach (a conclusion) by applying rules of logic or other forms of reasoning to given premises or known facts.
To examine, explain, or record (something) in an orderly manner.
ety: From Late Middle English deducen (“to demonstrate, prove, show; to argue, infer; to bring, lead; to turn (something) to a use; to deduct”), borrowed from Latin dēdūcere, the present active infinitive of dēdūcō (“to lead or bring out or away; to accompany, conduct, escort; (figuratively) to derive, discover, deduce”); from dē- (prefix meaning ‘from, away from’) + dūcere (the present active infinitive of dūcō (“to conduct, guide, lead; to draw, pull; to consider, regard, think”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to lead; to draw, pull”)).
examples: If you leave this Isle, and got to the court of England, see what regard there will be paid to the old pedigree that deduces your descent from kings and conquerors.

senses: An opinion, belief, or principle that is held as absolute truth by someone or especially an organization.
ety: Borrowed from Latin tenet (“he, she, or it holds”), from teneō (“hold; have”). Compare obsolete tenent. See tenable.
examples: Opposition to climate science has become not just the badge of honour for far-right politicians like Ukip’s Paul Nuttall. It has become the central tenet of their appeal to unreason.

senses: To put letters or words written in another writing system into the Latin (Roman) alphabet.
To bring under the authority or influence of Rome.
To make or become Roman in character or style.
To make or become Roman Catholic in religion (by conversion), character or style.
ety: From Roman + -ize.
examples: The author romanizes Chinese names using the Wade–Giles system rather than the Pinyin system.
A new system has been invented by which Chinese can be written in our letters as pronounced. This is called by the rather uncouth name of “Romanised.”
Some of the Chinese students had difficulty comprehending the need to Romanize the Chinese etymons.

senses: Of fluid motion, smooth and regular, flowing as though in different layers.
ety: From Latin lāmina (“thin sheet of material”) + English -ar.
examples: The laminar bands of color to the west bleeding out under the hammered clouds. A sudden violet-colored hooding of the earth.

senses: To make reparation, compensation, amends or satisfaction for an offence, crime, mistake or deficiency.
ety: From atone (“reconciled”), from Middle English atone, attone, atoon (“agreed”, literally “at one”), equivalent to at + one. Compare Latin adūnō (“to unite, make one”) for the similar formation. Regarding the different phonological development of atone and one, see the note in one.
examples: He tried to atone for his mistakes by working harder.
She gave a donation to atone for her past actions.
The ritual was performed to atone for sins.

senses: A form of horse-drawn carriage; a Blucher coach.
A sturdy laced leather half-boot.
ety: Named from Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher (1742–1819), a Prussian general.
examples: He whistled tunelessly his one air, beating his own time with a stick on the toe of his blucher, then looked overhead at the sun and calculated that she must have been lying like that for `close up an hour.'

senses: Survival as a Native American or First Nations person practicing indigenous culture and resisting white European-American hegemony.
The survival of Francophone culture in the face of Anglo-American hegemony.
Succession to an estate, office etc. of someone who survives the previous holder, as nominated by them; survivorship.
ety: From French survivance. In reference to Native Americans, sometimes alternatively interpreted as a blend of survival + resistance.
examples: One cannot appreciate and experience the power of Native survivance if the stories and memories of our histories are not placed within the context of struggle.
Joyfully existing as a queer Indigenous person is an act of survivance and reclamation of ancient ways of knowing who we are and how we love.
Joy Cedar (she/they) is a Two-Spirited poet, community worker, and visual artist. She incorporates survivance into the heart of her work. They live in Kentucky with their dog.

senses: Any organism, being or robot with six legs.
An arthropod with six feet; a member of subphylum Hexapoda.
ety: From hexa- + -pod, from Ancient Greek ἑξαποδ- (hexapod-), oblique stem of ἑξάπους (hexápous, “six-footed”), from ἑξα- (hexa-, “six”) + πούς (poús, “foot”).
examples: My lips will be even more firmly sealed about the various suggestions put forward concerning the interpersonal relationships of Alpha Centauri, the hermaphrodite hexapod.
The bizarre hexapods did indeed feed upon those unfortunate creatures who had been caught and killed by the flames. But the striped carnivores were not scavengers; They were hunters.
These concepts are applied to a robotic hexapod, which, through the use of compliant microspines on its feet, is capable of climbing hard vertical textured surfaces, such as stucco
